frequency_distribution_fitting.text: `monte_carlo_oprisk_capital` answers "how much operational risk capital is needed?": you give it a Poisson event rate (`frequency_lambda`) and lognormal severity settings (`severity_mu`, `severity_sigma`), and it simulates annual losses over `n_years`. It then reads the loss quantile at `confidence_level` (OpVaR) and reports capital as that quantile minus expected loss, along with expected shortfall. `frequency_distribution_fitting` answers an earlier question: "what event rate do my data support?" You give it observed annual loss-event counts (`annual_event_counts`), and it estimates the Poisson rate as the sample mean. It also reports a dispersion ratio, where a value far above 1 hints that a negative-binomial might suit better. In practice, the fitting function can supply the rate that you then enter as `frequency_lambda` in the Monte Carlo function.

explain.text: `monte_carlo_oprisk_capital` (Monte Carlo OpRisk Capital) simulates an operational risk loss distribution and returns regulatory capital. It builds annual losses by combining a Poisson event count (`frequency_lambda`) with lognormal severities (`severity_mu`, `severity_sigma`) over many simulated years (`n_years`). It reads the loss quantile at `confidence_level` as OpVaR (Basel AMA uses 99.9% over one year) and also reports expected shortfall. Capital is the unexpected loss, meaning OpVaR minus expected loss. Setting `seed` makes runs reproducible.

when.text:
`monte_carlo_oprisk_capital` (Monte Carlo OpRisk Capital) fits when you already have assumed frequency and severity inputs and want a simulated capital figure.

- You have a Poisson annual event rate (`frequency_lambda`) and lognormal severity parameters (`severity_mu`, `severity_sigma`) and want OpVaR and expected shortfall from them.
- You need capital defined as unexpected loss, meaning OpVaR minus expected loss, at a chosen `confidence_level` (the Basel AMA default is 99.9%).
- You want a reproducible simulation, using `seed` and `n_years` to control the run.
- You want to test how capital responds to different frequency or severity assumptions.
- If you only need the simulated aggregate annual loss distribution itself, `compound_loss_distribution` is listed as simulating that.
